clinicalPearls: Rare, severe congenital visceral myopathy defined by a massively distended, non-obstructed urinary bladder (megacystis), a narrow unused microcolon and intestinal hypoperistalsis.
In contrast to most neonatal obstructive disorders, it shows a female predominance.

The commonest cause is a heterozygous, usually de novo, variant in ACTG2, encoding smooth-muscle gamma-actin; autosomal recessive forms involve other contractile-apparatus genes such as MYH11, LMOD1, MYLK and MYL9.
Antenatal clues include an enlarged fetal bladder with upper urinary tract dilatation.
Neonates present with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, failure to pass meconium and functional urinary retention requiring catheterisation.
Enteric ganglion cells are present, which distinguishes the condition from Hirschsprung disease.
Most affected infants develop intestinal failure and become dependent on parenteral nutrition.
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome is a congenital visceral myopathy in which the smooth muscle of the bladder and gastrointestinal tract fails to generate effective contraction despite the absence of any mechanical obstruction. The commonest genetic cause is a heterozygous, usually de novo, variant in ACTG2, which encodes enteric smooth-muscle gamma-actin; such variants act in a dominant-negative fashion, impairing actin polymerisation and thus force generation. Autosomal recessive forms arise from biallelic variants in other genes of the contractile apparatus and its regulation, such as MYH11, LMOD1, MYLK and MYL9. The consequence is ineffective peristalsis: the bladder becomes massively distended and thin-walled with functional urinary retention and secondary upper-tract dilatation, while the small intestine shows hypoperistalsis or aperistalsis and the unused distal bowel remains narrow as a microcolon. Histology may reveal vacuolar degeneration of smooth muscle, at times with fibrosis, but enteric ganglion cells are characteristically preserved, which is central to distinguishing the condition from Hirschsprung disease.
additionalDifferentials: Hirschsprung disease (aganglionosis, whereas ganglion cells are present here)
Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction of other cause
Posterior urethral valves and other mechanical bladder outlet obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal and postnatal ultrasound of the bladder and urinary tract
Contrast studies demonstrating microcolon, malrotation and a functional, non-mechanical obstruction
Genetic testing beginning with ACTG2, followed by a panel for recessive visceral-myopathy genes
Full-thickness intestinal biopsy showing visceral myopathy with preserved ganglion cells
Rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease
redFlags: Bilious vomiting with abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium
Inability to establish enteral feeding and wean from parenteral nutrition
Recurrent central venous line sepsis and intestinal-failure-associated liver disease
Progressive upper urinary tract dilatation with declining renal function
reference.prognosis: Historically associated with high early mortality from intestinal failure, sepsis and complications of long-term parenteral nutrition. Survival has improved with contemporary intestinal-failure care and intestinal or multivisceral transplantation, although morbidity remains substantial.
pitfalls: Mistaking the functional obstruction for a mechanical one and performing futile bowel resections
Confusing the condition with Hirschsprung disease despite the presence of ganglion cells
Attributing the megacystis solely to urological outlet obstruction
Underusing antenatal bladder findings as an early diagnostic clue
references: Paediatric gastroenterology and intestinal failure references
management: Decompress the massively distended bladder with intermittent catheterisation or vesicostomy to relieve functional urinary retention and protect the upper renal tracts
Manage intestinal failure with total parenteral nutrition, attempting cautious enteral feeding as tolerated since prokinetic agents are generally ineffective in this visceral myopathy
Maintain meticulous central venous catheter care and treat line-associated and urinary sepsis promptly with appropriate antimicrobials
Use surgical measures such as decompressive or diverting stomas for the functional obstruction rather than expecting mechanical relief
Refer early to an intestinal-failure centre for consideration of isolated intestinal or multivisceral transplantation
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric surgical, urological, nutritional and gastroenterological care
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given the dominant ACTG2 and recessive contractile-apparatus gene causes
Escalate promptly for sepsis, upper urinary tract deterioration or parenteral-nutrition-associated liver disease
